Termination is permitted for mutual written consent; final prohibitory orders; failure of BRAC stockholder approval; failure of Conwall consent within ten business days after Form F-4 effectiveness; specified listing or reorganization failures; an uncured qualifying breach, subject to the applicable fifteen-day cure period; or failure of effectiveness or Closing by the Outside Date, subject to the agreement’s limitations on a materially breaching party. Upon termination, the agreement becomes void except for its surviving provisions and liability for specified pre-termination willful and material breaches. It does not address every holder or all state, local or non-U.S. taxes. Special rules apply to, among others, five-percent holders, the Sponsor and holders of founder or private securities, financial institutions, dealers, tax-exempt investors and compensatory holders. Investors should obtain advice for their own circumstances. Exchanges and cross-border limitations The parties intend that the July reorganization and the BRAC merger, considered together, qualify under Section 351 of the Internal Revenue Code and that the BRAC merger not trigger gain under Section 367(a)(1), subject to the applicable requirements. If that treatment applies, a qualifying U.S. holder generally would recognize no gain or loss on exchanging BRAC common shares for Holdco shares, carry over its aggregate basis, and include the holding period of the surrendered shares. Section 367 and its regulations impose additional conditions for transfers to a foreign corporation. A holder owning at least five percent of Holdco’s vote or value after the transaction may need a timely five-year gain recognition agreement and related compliance to avoid recognition of gain, but not loss. Satisfaction of the five-percent rules does not dispense with the other requirements of Sections 351 and 367. If the exchange is taxable because the intended treatment fails, a U.S. holder generally recognizes gain or loss equal to the fair market value of the Holdco shares received less the basis of the surrendered shares; its new basis generally equals fair market value and its new holding period begins the following day. Capital-loss limitations and holder-specific rules apply. The July reorganization, September share changes, advisory transfers and all Closing issuances must be considered in the transaction-specific analysis. Rights holders and Covered Loan creditors require separate analysis of their particular instruments; the common-share discussion does not establish their tax treatment. Redemptions A cash redemption is generally analyzed under Section 302 as a sale or exchange if the applicable substantially disproportionate, complete-termination or not-essentially-equivalent-to-a-dividend test is met, taking account of constructive ownership, including relevant rights. Sale treatment generally produces capital gain or loss equal to cash received less basis. Otherwise, Section 301 generally treats the payment as a dividend to the extent of earnings and profits, then as a reduction of basis and then gain. A holder that redeems all shares and receives no Holdco shares ordinarily is not exposed to Holdco’s PFIC rules or Section 367 solely through the merger; a partial redeemer receiving Holdco shares may be. Holdco PFIC risk and information BRAC is a domestic corporation and is not a PFIC. Holdco is foreign and may be a PFIC for a year if at least 75% of gross income is passive or at least 50% of assets produce or are held to produce passive income, subject to the applicable look-through rules. Status is determined annually and depends on actual income, assets, valuations and the use of cash. No assurance is given that Holdco or a relevant subsidiary will not be a PFIC. Absent an effective qualified electing fund or mark-to-market election where available, gains and excess distributions can be subject to adverse allocation, tax-rate and interest-charge rules. Elections, information reporting, dividends and subsequent disposals are subject to holder-specific requirements. The agreement provides for PFIC determinations and commercially reasonable efforts to supply applicable annual information statements within the specified framework, including a 120-day determination period after the relevant year-end. This covenant does not guarantee availability or effectiveness of any investor election. Backup withholding and information-reporting rules may also apply. Tax analysis and opinions No transaction-specific U.S. tax opinion is included in this registration statement. The intended treatment is an objective rather than an opinion that the applicable requirements have been met, and Closing is not conditioned on receipt of such an opinion. No IRS ruling has been requested or is intended. CCISB reports that it has no U.S. holders and does not foresee material U.S. federal income tax consequences of the Business Combination to its pre-merger stockholders on that basis. This limited statement does not establish the entity-level tax consequences to BRAC, Holdco or CCISB, or the treatment of BRAC rights, debt conversion or redemption excise tax, which require completed transaction-specific analysis by U.S. tax counsel. The parties intend to engage U.S. tax counsel to provide the required transaction-specific opinion and consent with a subsequent Form F-4 amendment. Neither is included in the supplied draft, and no tax-treatment conclusion is represented as having been delivered. We believe we will be able to meet these costs through the use of funds to be loaned by or invested in us by our stockholders, management or other investors. Our management and stockholders have indicated their intent to advance funds on behalf of the Company as needed in order to accomplish its business plan and comply with its Exchange Act reporting requirements; however, there are no agreements in effect between the Company and our management and stockholders specifically requiring that they provide any funds to the Company. Any future loans from officers, directors, sponsors or affiliates may be evidenced by promissory notes, may be unsecured, may bear interest or be non-interest bearing, and may be repayable upon completion of a business combination or other future financing event. As a result, there are no assurances that such funds will be advanced or that the Company will be able to secure any additional funding as needed. The analysis of new business opportunities will be undertaken by or under the supervision of the Company’s management. As of the date of this filing, the Company has entered into a Business Combination agreement with Conwall. While the Company has limited assets and no revenues, the Company has unrestricted flexibility in seeking, analyzing and participating in potential business opportunities in that it may seek out a target company in any type of business, industry or geographical location. In its efforts to analyze potential acquisition targets, the Company will consider the following kinds of factors: (a) potential for growth, indicated by new technology, anticipated market expansion or new products; (b) competitive position as compared to other firms of similar size and experience within the industry segment as well as within the industry as a whole; 17 (c) strength and diversity of management, either in place or scheduled for recruitment; (d) capital requirements and anticipated availability of required funds, to be provided by the Company or from operations, through the sale of additional securities, through joint ventures or similar arrangements or from other sources; (e) the cost of participation by the Company as compared to the perceived tangible and intangible values and potentials; (f) the extent to which the business opportunity can be advanced; and (g) the accessibility of required management expertise, personnel, raw materials, services, professional assistance and other required items. In applying the foregoing criteria, no one of which will be definitive, management will attempt to analyze all factors and circumstances and make a determination based upon reasonable investigative measures and available data. Potentially available business opportunities may occur in many different industries, and at various stages of development, all of which will make the task of comparative investigation and analysis of such business opportunities extremely difficult and complex. Due to the Registrant’s limited capital available for investigation, the Registrant may not discover or adequately evaluate adverse facts about the opportunity to be acquired. In addition, we will be competing against other entities that possess greater financial, technical and managerial capabilities for identifying and completing business combinations. In evaluating a prospective business combination, we will conduct as extensive a due diligence review of potential targets as possible given the lack of information which may be available regarding private companies and our limited personnel and financial resources. We expect that our due diligence will encompass, among other things, meetings with the target business’s incumbent management and inspection of its facilities, as necessary, as well as a review of financial and other information which is made available to us. This due diligence review will be conducted either by our management or by unaffiliated third parties we may engage, including but not limited to attorneys, accountants, consultants or other such professionals. The costs associated with hiring third parties as required to complete a business combination may be significant and are difficult to determine as such costs may vary depending on a variety of factors, including the amount of time it takes to complete a business combination, the location of the target company, and the size and complexity of the business of the target company. Our limited funds and the lack of full-time management will likely make it impracticable to conduct a complete and exhaustive investigation and analysis of a target business before we consummate a business combination. Management decisions, therefore, will likely be made without detailed feasibility studies, independent analysis, market surveys and the like, which, if we had more funds available to us, would be desirable. We will be particularly dependent in making decisions upon information provided by the promoters, owners, sponsors or others associated with the target business seeking our participation. The time and costs required to select and evaluate a target business and to structure and complete a business combination cannot presently be ascertained with any degree of certainty. The amount of time it takes to complete a business combination, the location of the target company, and the size and complexity of the business of the target company, whether current stockholders of the Company will retain equity in the Company, the scope of the due diligence investigation required, the involvement of the Company’s auditors in the transaction, possible changes in the Company’s capital structure in connection with the transaction, and whether funds may be raised contemporaneously with the transaction are all factors that determine the costs associated with completing a business combination transaction. The time and costs required to complete a business combination can be estimated once a business combination target has been identified. Any costs incurred with respect to the evaluation of a prospective business combination that is not ultimately completed will result in a loss to us. Through information obtained from industry professionals including attorneys, investment bankers, and other consultants with experience in the reverse merger industry, the Company is aware that there are hundreds of shell companies seeking a business combination target. As a result, the Company believes it is in a highly competitive market for a small number of business opportunities which could reduce the likelihood of consummating a successful business combination. We are, and will continue to be, an insignificant participant in the business of seeking mergers with, joint ventures with and acquisitions of small private and public entities. A large number of established and well-financed entities, including small public companies and venture capital firms, are active in mergers and acquisitions of companies that may be desirable target candidates for us. Nearly all these entities have significantly greater financial resources, technical expertise and managerial capabilities than we do; consequently, we will be at a competitive disadvantage in identifying possible business opportunities and successfully completing a business combination. These competitive factors may reduce the likelihood of our identifying and consummating a successful business combination. 18 None of BRAC’s current directors or executive officers is presently involved in any other blank-check company. They may become associated with another blank-check company in the future, which could create conflicts in allocating business opportunities. In evaluating opportunities among entities with which management may become affiliated, management would consider applicable fiduciary duties, the stage of transaction development, industry focus, capital requirements, target company preferences and other relevant factors. At this time, the Company has not identified any specific factors or criteria that will be used to determine which entity will proceed with a proposed transaction in the event of a conflict of interest and management reserves the right to use any such criteria as it determines to be relevant at the time a proposed transaction is presented. However, in the event a conflict of interest arises in connection with the identification of a proposed business transaction, the Company’s management and board of directors will use its reasonable judgment and intends to take all such actions as may be required in order to satisfy its fiduciary duties. At this time, there are no specific conflicts of interests identified by our management. We presently have no employees apart from our management. Our officers and directors are engaged in outside business activities and are employed on a full-time basis by other companies. Our officers and directors will be dividing their time amongst these entities and anticipate that they will devote very limited time to our business until the acquisition of a successful business opportunity has been identified. We anticipate that our officers will devote on average approximately 5 to 10 hours per week to the Company’s operations, including corporate governance, regulatory compliance and identifying potential business opportunities. Management anticipates that this time commitment may increase as the Company moves closer to identifying and executing a business combination. The specific amount of time that management will devote to the Company may vary from week to week or even day to day, and therefore the specific amount of time that management will devote to the Company on a weekly basis cannot be ascertained with any level of certainty. In all cases, management intends to spend as much time as is necessary to exercise their fiduciary duties as an officer and/or director of the Company and believes that they will be able to devote the time required to consummate a business combination transaction as necessary. We expect no significant changes in the number of our employees other than such changes, if any, incident to a business combination. Form of Acquisition The manner in which the Registrant participates in an opportunity will depend upon the nature of the opportunity, the respective needs and desires of the Registrant and the promoters of the opportunity, and the relative negotiating strength of the Registrant and such promoters. It is likely that the Registrant will acquire its participation in a business opportunity through the issuance of its Common Stock or other securities of the Registrant, which could result in substantial dilution to the equity of stockholders of the Registrant immediately prior to the consummation of a transaction. The proposed Conwall transaction is governed by the amended Business Combination Agreement. Its intended tax treatment is subject to applicable legal requirements and the facts at Closing. It should be noted that the criteria for determining whether an acquisition is a so-called “tax-free” reorganization under Section 368(a)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the “Code”), depend upon the transaction meeting certain statutory and non-statutory requirements. There are different statutory requirements for each type of tax-free reorganization, and each transaction must be reviewed carefully to determine its eligibility. One statutory requirement in a tax-free reorganization is that at least a certain percentage of the total consideration must be voting stock of the acquirer corporation. This could result in substantial dilution to the equity of those who were stockholders of the Registrant before the reorganization. In addition, post-transaction dispositions of Registrant stock received as consideration could have implications for the tax-free nature of the transaction. The Company will file a current report on Form 8-K, as required, within four business days of a Business Combination that results in the Company ceasing to be a shell company. This Form 8-K will include complete disclosure of the target company, including audited financial statements. The present stockholders of the Registrant will likely not have control of a majority of the voting securities of the Registrant following a reorganization transaction. As part of such a transaction, all or a majority of the Registrant’s directors may resign and one or more new directors may be appointed without any vote by stockholders. In the case of an acquisition, the transaction may be accomplished upon the sole determination of management without any vote or approval by stockholders. In the case of a statutory merger or consolidation directly involving the Company, it will likely be necessary to call a stockholders’ meeting and obtain the approval of the holders of a majority of the outstanding securities. The necessity to obtain such stockholder approval may result in delay and additional expense in the consummation of any proposed transaction and will also give rise to certain appraisal rights to dissenting stockholders. Emerging Growth Company The Company is an “emerging growth company”, as defined in the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act of 2012 (“JOBS Act”), and may take advantage of certain exemptions from various reporting requirements that are applicable to other public companies that are not “emerging growth companies” including, but not limited to, not being required to comply with the auditor attestation requirements of section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, and exemptions from the requirements of Sections 14A(a) and (b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 to hold a nonbinding advisory vote of stockholders on executive compensation and any golden parachute payments not previously approved. The Company has elected to use the extended transition period for complying with new or revised accounting standards under Section 102(b)(1) of the JOBS Act. This election allows us to delay the adoption of new or revised accounting standards that have different effective dates for public and private companies until those standards apply to private companies. As a result of this election, our financial statements may not be comparable to companies that comply with public company effective dates. Our emerging growth company status is subject to the statutory five-year limit following our initial public offering and may end earlier if our annual gross revenues are $1.235 billion or more, we issue more than $1 billion of non-convertible debt in a three-year period, or we become a large accelerated filer under Exchange Act Rule 12b-2. To the extent that we continue to qualify as a “smaller reporting company”, as such term is defined in Rule 12b-2 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, after we cease to qualify as an emerging growth company, certain of the exemptions available to us as an emerging growth company may continue to be available to us as a smaller reporting company, including: (1) not being required to comply with the auditor attestation requirements of Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes Oxley Act; (2) scaled executive compensation disclosures; and (3) the requirement to provide only two years of audited financial statements, instead of three years. Shell Company Status We are a “shell company” as defined in Rule 405 of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”) and Rule 12b-2 under the Exchange Act. The term shell company means a registrant, other than an asset-backed issuer as defined in Item 1101(b) of Regulation AB, that has no or nominal operations and either no or nominal assets, assets consisting solely of cash and cash equivalents, or assets consisting of any amount of cash and cash equivalents and nominal other assets. Some of the consequences of being a shell company are as follows: ◌ Rule 145a under the Securities Act provides that any direct or indirect business combination of a reporting shell company (that is not a business combination related shell company as defined in Rule 405) involving another entity that is not a shell company is deemed to involve an offer, offer to sell, offer for sale, or sale within the meaning of section 2(a)(3) of the Securities Act of securities to the reporting shell company’s existing shareholders. Where Rule 145a applies, that deemed offer and sale would need to be registered under the Securities Act, unless there is an applicable exemption. The proposed Conwall Business Combination contemplates a separate registration statement on Form F-4 covering the transaction. This Form 10 registers BRAC’s common stock under the Exchange Act and does not itself register the offer or sale of the transaction securities under the Securities Act. 21 ◌ The applicable rules of the SEC prohibit the use of Form S-8 under the Securities Act (for registration of securities of the registrant to be offered under employee benefit plans to its directors, officers, employees and consultants) by shell companies until 60 days after the registrant ceases to be a shell company. ◌ Form 8-K under the Exchange Act requires a shell company (other than a business combination related shell company) that is reporting an acquisition of a business or change of control that causes it to cease being a shell company to disclose the same information, giving effect to the transaction, that it would be required to provide in registering a class of securities under the Exchange Act, including financial statements and pro forma financial information of an acquired business (a so-called “Super 8-K”) within four business days after completing the transaction. We anticipate filing such a Super 8-K upon completing a prospective business combination. ◌ Rule 15-01 of Regulation S-X provides for specific financial statement requirements applicable to acquisitions involving shell companies (other than business combination related shell companies). ◌ Pursuant to Rule 144(i) “restricted” securities (generally, securities acquired directly or indirectly from the issuer, or from an affiliate of the issuer, in a transaction or chain of transactions not involving any public offering) and “control” securities (generally, securities held by an affiliate of the issuer) issued by a current or former shell company that otherwise meet the holding period and other requirements for resale under Rule 144 nevertheless cannot be sold in reliance on Rule 144 until one year after the issuer (a) is no longer a shell company and (b) has filed current “Form 10 information” (as defined in Rule 144(i)) with the SEC reflecting that it is no longer a shell company, and provided that at the time of a proposed sale pursuant to Rule 144, the issuer is subject to the reporting requirements of Section 13 or 15(d) of the Exchange Act and has filed all reports and other materials required to be filed by Section 13 or 15(d) of the Exchange Act, as applicable, during the preceding twelve months, other than Form 8-K reports. As a result, restrictive legends on certificates or book-entry positions for our shares that are “restricted” or “control” securities cannot be removed except in connection with (i) an actual sale meeting the foregoing requirements or (ii) pursuant to an effective registration statement. We anticipate that the Super 8-K that we would file upon completing a prospective business combination would contain the required current “Form 10 information.” As a shell company, the Company may experience difficulty attracting potential acquisition candidates, obtaining financing, maintaining service providers, and developing a trading market for its securities, Blank Check Company We are a “blank check company” as defined under Rule 419 of the Securities Act, as amended. Rule 419 imposes certain restrictive requirements on offerings of securities by blank check companies. However, we have no present intention of engaging in an offering of our securities that would be subject to Rule 419 while we remain a blank check company. We anticipate raising funds through an offering of our securities only upon completion of a business combination as a result of which we would no longer be a blank check company. Therefore, we do not anticipate that the provisions of Rule 419 will deter a potential target company from entering into a business combination transaction with us. Following effectiveness of this registration statement, we intend to maintain compliance with Exchange Act reporting requirements. We may seek quotation of our securities on an over-the-counter market; however, there can be no assurance that a market maker will file an application for quotation, that quotation will be approved, or that an active trading market will develop. 22 Conwall Business Holdco Corporate Structure Holdco is an exempted company with limited liability incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands on 12 February 2026 solely for the purpose of effectuating the Business Combination described herein. Regulatory framework and compliance exposure Conwall’s Malaysian operations are subject to contractor registration and project declarations under the CIDB framework; building completion and occupancy requirements; local premises and advertising licenses; employment, immigration and foreign-worker approvals; workplace safety and health duties; and statutory provident-fund, social-security, employment-insurance and minimum-wage obligations. These requirements affect tender eligibility, deployment of workers, occupation of premises and project execution. The detailed applicable laws and disclosed requirements follow in “Government and Industry Regulations.” Project performance also involves environmental and site controls, waste and pollution requirements, anti-bribery obligations, and protection of employee, customer and project information. Cybersecurity incidents, mishandled personal data, corrupt payments or regulatory noncompliance could result in claims, investigation, remediation costs, loss of licenses or project eligibility, and reputational damage. The terminated local CIDB registration, pending foreign registration and Ipoh license application described above are specific compliance exposures and are not covered by a blanket statement of compliance. Compliance entails registration and renewal fees, levies, employee contributions, safety personnel and training, monitoring and remediation costs. These costs are included in the appropriate operating or project expenses; the financial information included here does not separately quantify a comprehensive compliance-cost amount. The CIDB regime described below imposes a 0.125% levy on construction work exceeding RM500,000, subject to applicable exemptions. The financial statements do not isolate actual levy and other compliance expenditures; the statutory rate is not an estimate of total compliance cost. Pending licensing matters may generate additional costs or operating restrictions that have not been quantified. This disclosure should be read with the specific regulatory and licensing matters above and the contingencies notes to its financial statements. It does not eliminate risks from ordinary-course construction claims, liquidated damages, customer disputes, labor matters or tax examinations. As of June 30, 2026, CCISB had completed 53 construction and facility infrastructure projects, each with a contract price of at least $24,038 (RM100,000), since commencing operations in 2021 and had 12 additional projects in progress. Our projects are primarily located in Malaysia, where we have established experience and relationships with customers in the semiconductor and advanced manufacturing sectors. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 and the three months ended June 30, 2026, all of our revenue was generated from projects in Malaysia, and we did not generate any revenue from outside Malaysia during these periods. See “Risk Factors — All of our revenue is generated in Malaysia, and our planned expansion into other Southeast Asian markets may not succeed.” and “Risk Factors — Customer concentration, project concentration and non-recurring project revenue may cause significant volatility in our results.” Competition We operate in an increasingly competitive industry that is rapidly evolving. We compete with specialized engineering and cleanroom infrastructure contractors such as Polycool THE Engineering Sdn Bhd, IAQ Engineering Sdn Bhd and Hong Poh Engineering Sdn Bhd. We believe the principal competitive factors in our market include semiconductor project expertise; the ability to manage technically complex projects without compromising manufacturing readiness; schedule reliability; cleanroom and contamination-control capabilities; process utility and M&E expertise; experience in supporting advanced packaging capabilities; access to skilled and qualified personnel; established supplier and procurement networks; and local presence and customer relationships. 26 We believe we compete favorably on the factors described above. In particular, we believe our competitive strengths include our experience in high-technology facility infrastructure projects, particularly for semiconductor and advanced manufacturing customers, our ability to integrate cleanroom, process utility and M&E works, and our track record of delivering technically complex projects within customers’ required schedules. Since commencing our construction and maintenance services in 2021, we have completed 53 construction and facility infrastructure projects, each with a contract price of at least $24,038 (RM100,000), and had 12 additional projects in progress as of June 30, 2026. We also believe our established customer relationships, understanding of semiconductor facility requirements and ability to coordinate multiple engineering and construction disciplines enable us to respond effectively to customers’ project requirements and support timely project delivery. In addition, we have developed a broad sourcing network across East Asia, which enables us to identify and procure equipment, materials and other project resources from a wider range of suppliers and may provide us with cost competitiveness in project execution. Despite our competitive strengths, we anticipate that larger Malaysian general contractors and construction groups may directly compete with us for projects. Many of our current and potential competitors have longer operating histories, greater financial resources, bonding capacity and large-project execution experience. These factors, together with uncertainty regarding customer investment, procurement decisions and semiconductor cyclicality, may intensify competition and lead competitors to adopt lower prices, making it difficult for us to secure projects on acceptable terms. If we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition and results of operations will be adversely affected. See “Risk Factors — Competition from specialized M&E contractors and larger general contractors may reduce project awards, pricing and margins.” and “Risk Factors — We compete for project awards on the basis of a limited number of reference projects and customer qualifications, and we may be unable to win new work on commercially acceptable terms.” Insurance CCISB maintains insurance coverage that it believes is relevant for its businesses and operations. The Company maintains commercial general liability, motor vehicle insurance, workmen’s compensation, construction insurance covering contractor all risks and erection all risks, public liability insurance, employee insurance covering term life, crisis cover, accidental death, accidental medical, among other coverage. We also purchase fire, burglary and business insurance, covering our inventory and fixed assets such as equipment and tools of trade. We also maintain business inconvenience insurance. We believe that our insurance coverage is in line with industry standards and is adequate to cover our key assets, facilities and liabilities. See “Risk Factors — Failure to comply with environmental, workplace safety, building, construction, tax, labor or licensing regulations could adversely affect our operations.” and “Risk Factors — Changes in Malaysian government policy, taxation and licensing requirements could increase our costs or restrict our ability to bid for projects.” Lembaga Pembangunan Industri Pembinaan Malaysia Act 1994 (“CIDB Act 1994”) The CIDB Act 1994 governs the establishment of CIDB and provides for its function in relation to the construction industry and all matters connected therewith. Pursuant to Section 25(1) of the CIDB Act 1994, a person may not carry out or undertake construction work, or hold itself out as a contractor, unless it is registered with CIDB and holds a valid certificate of registration issued by CIDB. Under Section 29 of the CIDB Act 1994, any person who contravenes Section 25(1) commits an offence and shall, on conviction, be liable to a fine of not less than RM10,000 and not more than RM100,000. 28 In this regard, contractors must comply with various regulatory requirements imposed under the CIDB Act 1994, including obligations relating to the declaration and submission of construction contracts awarded to them, as well as the payment of levy to CIDB in respect of construction contracts exceeding RM500,000 at the prescribed rate of 0.125% of the contract sum. Contractors are further required to fully disclose all information affecting their levy obligations and to comply with prescribed timelines for such submissions. Failure to comply with such requirements may result in the imposition of fines of up to RM50,000 or other penalties as prescribed under the CIDB Act 1994. In addition, Section 34B of the CIDB Act 1994 imposes general duties on contractors undertaking construction works, including the obligation to submit information and supporting documents relating to construction works as required by CIDB, to ensure compliance with the CIDB Act 1994 and all applicable laws, regulations and conditions imposed by CIDB, and to ensure the safety of construction works during and after completion. CCISB then applied for foreign-contractor registration; the application remains pending, and its timing, grade, categories, specializations and conditions are uncertain. The terminated local CIDB certificate stated a validity period from May 6, 2026 to July 27, 2029; that printed expiry date does not establish current authority following its October 5, 2026 termination. Under the terms and conditions of its registration, the Company is required, among others, to comply with CIDB Act 1994 and all regulations, conditions and restrictions imposed by CIDB from time to time, undertake construction works only within its registered categories and specialisations, submit notifications and information relating to construction contracts within the prescribed timeframe, display its registration details as required, ensure compliance with applicable codes of conduct and ethics, and appoint appropriately skilled and accredited construction personnel and site supervisors. The Company is also required to ensure that all construction personnel at its sites possess valid CIDB Construction Personnel Cards. CIDB may suspend, revoke or cancel a contractor’s registration in the event of non-compliance with applicable laws, breach of registration conditions, provision of false or misleading information, abandonment of construction works without reasonable cause, or other prescribed grounds under the CIDB Act 1994 and its regulations. The July 16, 2026 share swap placed CCISB under the ownership of Cayman Islands Holdco. Street, Drainage and Building Act 1974 (“SDBA 1974”) and Uniform Building By-Laws 1984 (“UBBL 1984”) The SDBA 1974 regulate laws relating to street, drainage and buildings in local authority areas in Peninsular Malaysia. It provides for the requirement to have a Certificate of Fitness for Occupation (“CFO”) or a Certificate of Completion and Compliance (“CCC”) to ensure that a building is safe and fit for occupation. UBBL 1984 has been put into force pursuant to the exercise of the powers conferred by the SDBA 1974. Under the UBBL 1984, a CFO or a CCC in respect of a building shall be issued upon satisfaction of amongst others, the following requirements: (a) the qualified persons (i.e. the architect, registered building draughtsman or engineer) (“Qualified Persons”) have certified that they have supervised the erection of the building and that the building has been constructed in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations and any conditions imposed by the local authority; (b) the building has been constructed in accordance with the UBBL 1984 and any conditions imposed by the local authority have been satisfied; (c) the Qualified Persons accept full responsibility for those portions which they are respectively concerned with; and (d) all essential services have been provided. Any person who occupies or permits to be occupied any building or any part thereof without a CFO/CCC shall be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding RM250,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 10 years or to both. 29 Local Government Act 1976 (“LGA 1976”) Pursuant to Section 102 of the LGA 1976, local authorities in Malaysia are empowered to regulate and supervise trades, businesses and industries within their respective jurisdictions through the issuance of by-laws, including licensing requirements for business premises and related activities. Under Section 107 of the LGA 1976 and the relevant local authority by-laws, no person may carry out any trade or business or use any premises for business purposes without obtaining a valid business premise licence issued by the relevant local authority. In addition, where applicable, separate licences may be required for the display of advertisements or signage at business premises. In Johor Bahru, the Company’s operations are subject to the Undang-Undang Kecil Pelesenan Tred, Perniagaan dan Perindustrian (Majlis Bandaraya Johor Bahru) 2016 and the Undang-Undang Kecil Pelesenan Iklan (Majlis Bandaraya Johor Bahru) 2010. These by-laws require that no person shall use any premises within the Johor Bahru City Council area for any trade, business or industrial activity, or exhibit any advertisement, without first obtaining the requisite licence issued by the Mayor. The Johor Bahru by-laws also empower the local authority to impose licence conditions, require compliance with specified requirements, and order the closure of any premises operating without a valid licence until such licence is obtained or renewed. Non-compliance with these requirements constitutes an offence and may result in a fine not exceeding RM2,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding one (1) year, or both, and in the case of a continuing offence, a further fine not exceeding RM200 for each day during which the offence continues after conviction. Under the Licence Fees By-Laws 1980, it is an offence to operate any licensable item specified in the schedules thereto without a valid licence issued by the President of the Council, and any contravention of the said by-laws or of any condition imposed thereunder is punishable by a fine not exceeding RM2,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding one (1) year, or both, and in the case of a continuing offence, a further fine not exceeding RM200 for each day during which the offence continues after conviction. Under the Advertisement By-Laws 2001, no advertisement may be exhibited except under and in accordance with a licence issued by the Council, and any contravention of the said by-laws or of any notice or order of the Council is punishable by a fine not exceeding RM2,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding one (1) year, or both. Where the Council approves the retention of an advertisement which has been exhibited without a licence, a fee equivalent to three (3) times the annual license fee is payable, and the Council may in addition order the removal or erasure of the advertisement and recover the costs of removal from the person in default. Employment Act 1955 (“EA 1955”), Employment (Restriction) Act 1968 (Revised 2017) (“ERA 1968”) and Immigration Act 1959/63 (“Immigration Act”) The employment of foreign workers in Malaysia is principally governed by EA 1955, ERA 1968 and the Immigration Act. These laws regulate, among others, the employment of foreign employees, the requirement to obtain valid employment permits and immigration passes, and the obligations of employers engaging foreign workers in Malaysia. Pursuant to Section 60K of the EA 1955, an employer is prohibited from employing a foreign employee unless prior approval has been obtained from the Director General of Labor. An employer who contravenes this requirement commits an offence and shall, upon conviction, be liable to a fine not exceeding RM100,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding five (5) years or both. In addition, Section 5 of the ERA 1968 prohibits the employment of a non-citizen in Malaysia unless a valid employment permit has been issued in respect of such non-citizen. Any person who fails to comply with this requirement commits an offence and shall, upon conviction, be liable to a fine not exceeding RM5,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding one (1) year or both. The Immigration Act further regulates the entry and employment of non-citizens in Malaysia. Under Section 55B of the Immigration Act, any person who employs one or more persons, other than a citizen or holder of a valid entry permit, who are not in possession of a valid pass commits an offence and shall, upon conviction, be liable to a fine of not less than RM10,000 and not more than RM50,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding twelve (12) months or both for each such employee. Where more than five (5) such employees are employed, additional penalties, including imprisonment, may be imposed under the Immigration Act. The Company’s operations require the employment of both local and foreign workers. As of the date of this registration statement, the Company had a total workforce of 54 employees, comprising 50 local employees and 4 foreign employees. The foreign employees are employed pursuant to valid work permits, employment passes and/or other immigration documents, which are renewable in accordance with the applicable laws and regulations. We believe that we have complied in all material respects with the requirements of the EA 1955, ERA 1968 and the Immigration Act relating to the employment of foreign workers. As of the date of this registration statement, we are not aware of any material non-compliance with these laws that would have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition or results of operations. Occupational Safety and Health Act 1994 (“OSHA 1994”) The OSHA 1994 establishes the framework for securing the safety, health and welfare of persons at work and for protecting other persons against risks to safety or health arising from work activities. Under the OSHA 1994, employers are required to ensure, so far as is practicable, the safety, health and welfare of their employees while at work. These obligations include providing and maintaining safe systems of work, ensuring the safe use, operation, handling, storage and transportation of plant and substances, providing adequate information, instruction, training and supervision to employees, maintaining a safe working environment, implementing emergency procedures, conducting workplace risk assessments and adopting appropriate risk control measures. The OSHA 1994 further requires employers to prepare and maintain a written occupational safety and health policy and to communicate such policy to employees. Employers are also required to notify the Department of Occupational Safety and Health (“DOSH”) of the occupation or use of premises as a place of work where applicable. In addition, where prescribed under the OSHA 1994 and its subsidiary legislation, employers are required to appoint competent and registered safety and health officers and establish safety and health committees at their workplaces. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in fines, imprisonment or both. In particular, contravention of certain provisions relating to occupational safety and health policies, workplace risk assessments and employer duties may result in penalties of up to RM500,000 or imprisonment for a term of up to two (2) years or both. 31 As a company engaged in construction-related activities, occupational safety and health compliance forms an important part of the Company’s operations. The Company has adopted a written occupational safety and health policy and has implemented occupational safety, health and environmental procedures designed to promote compliance with the OSHA 1994 and applicable regulations. The Company also conducts workplace risk assessments and implements appropriate control measures to manage occupational safety and health risks arising from its operations. As of the date of this registration statement, the Company has appointed competent personnel to oversee occupational safety and health matters and has established a safety and health committee in accordance with the applicable requirements under the OSHA 1994. The Company has also submitted the requisite notice of occupation to DOSH and maintains the relevant occupational safety and health documentation required for its operations. Employees’ Provident Fund Act 1991 (“EPFA 1991”) The EPFA 1991 imposes the statutory obligations on employers and employees to make contributions towards the Employees Provident Fund, which is essentially a fund established as a scheme of savings for employees’ retirement and the management of savings for retirement purposes. Pursuant to section 43(1) of the EPFA 1991, it is compulsory for employees and their employers to make monthly contributions on the amount of wages at the rate respectively set out in the Third Schedule of the EPFA. Any employer who fails to pay the necessary contributions to the account of the individual employee shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 years or to a fine not exceeding RM10,000 or to both. As of the date of this registration statement, the Company has made the required contributions towards the Employees Provident Fund and is in compliance with the EPFA 1991 and all regulations made thereunder. Employees’ Social Security Act 1969 (“ESSA 1969”) The ESSA 1969 was implemented to provide protection for employees and their dependents against economic and social distress in the event of invalidity, disablement or employment injury. The schemes of social security under the 1969 Act are administered by Social Security Organization (“SOCSO”) and are financed by compulsory contributions made by the employers and the employees. All employees, in industries to which the SOCSO Act applies are required to be insured. It is the obligation of the employer to pay the contribution (both the employer’s contribution and the employee’s contribution) to SOCSO at the rates set out in Third Schedule of ESSA 1969. Pursuant to ESSA 1969, any person being an employer who fails to pay any contributions which he is liable under the ESSA 1969 to pay in respect of or on behalf of any employee shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 2 years, or with fine not exceeding RM10,000, or with both. As of the date of this registration statement, the Company has made the required contributions under the ESSA 1969 and is in compliance with the ESSA 1969 and all regulations made thereunder. Employment Insurance System Act 2017 (“EISA 2017”) The EISA 2017 provides for the establishment of an employment insurance system (“EIS”) administered by SOCSO to provide certain benefits and a re-employment placement program for insured persons in the event of loss of employment which will promote active labor market policies. All employees in the industries to which the EISA 2017 applies shall be registered and insured by the employers. Under the EISA 2017, both employers and employees (from 18 to 59 years of age) are required to contribute to the EIS with the rates, subject to the revision by the Minister, as specified in the Second Schedule based on the amount of the monthly wages of the employee. Employees who have attained the age of 60, or employees who have attained the age of 57 and have never made contributions under the EISA 2017 before attaining the age of 57, are exempted from this protection plan. An insured person who considers that he has lost his employment shall submit an application to claim for benefits up to 6 months to SOCSO within 60 days from the date he considers that he has lost his employment. After considering if the contributions qualifying conditions are fulfilled (the fulfillment of which depends on the number of past claims and contributions made preceding to the loss of employment) in respect of a claim for benefits by an insured person, SOCSO may approve or reject the claim for benefits. 32 Minimum Wages Order 2024 Pursuant to the Minimum Wages Order 2024, the minimum wage for employees shall be RM1,700 a month. Under the National Wages Consultative Council Act 2011, failure to comply with the minimum wage requirement may result in a fine of not more than RM10,000 imposed on the employer for each employee. If an employer is a body corporate, any person who at the time of the commission of the offence was a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer of the body corporate may be charged severally or jointly in the same proceedings with the body corporate and if the body corporate is found to have committed the offence, shall be deemed to have committed that offence unless, having regard to the nature of his functions in that capacity and to all circumstances, he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge, consent or connivance; and that he had taken all reasonable precautions and exercised due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence. The Malaysian court may also order the employer to pay each employee the difference between statutory minimum wages and the employee’s basic wages paid by the employer to the employee, including outstanding differences. Risk Factors. As a “smaller reporting company” as defined in Item 10 of Regulation S-K (17 C.F.R. §229.10(f)(1)), the Company is not required to provide the information called for by this Item. However, the Company has elected to provide the following risk factor disclosure for the benefit of investors. An investment in our securities involves a high degree of risk. You should carefully consider the following risk factors, together with all of the other information included in this registration statement, before making an investment decision. If any of the following risks actually occur, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be materially and adversely affected. Risks Relating to Our Status as a Shell Company We are a blank check company with no operating history and no revenues, and you will not have a basis for evaluating our ability to achieve our business objective. We are a blank check company incorporated under the laws of the State of Delaware with no operating history and no revenues. We were formed for the purpose of effecting a merger, capital stock exchange, asset acquisition, stock purchase, reorganization, or similar business combination with one or more businesses. Because we lack an operating history, you have no basis upon which to evaluate our ability to achieve our business objective of completing an initial business combination. We have not conducted any operations other than organizational activities, activities relating to our initial public offering, and activities directed toward identifying and evaluating prospective acquisition candidates. We may never generate any operating revenues or profits. Our sole activities since inception have been organizational activities, including the identification of potential target businesses. We have not generated any revenues from operations to date and do not expect to generate operating revenues until after the completion of our initial business combination. We have no present revenue and will not generate any revenue until, at the earliest, after the consummation of a business combination. Our ability to commence operations is contingent upon obtaining adequate financial resources through a business combination. Since we do not have an operating history and have not generated any revenues, investors have no basis for evaluating our ability to achieve our stated business objective. We cannot assure you that the funds remaining in the trust account after satisfaction of all obligations will be sufficient to provide shareholders with a meaningful return on their investment, particularly after giving effect to any reduction in trust account value during the period of our operations. Risks Relating to Limited Cash Resources We have limited cash resources outside of the trust account, which may be insufficient to fund our operations and pursuit of a business combination. The proceeds of our initial public offering were placed into a trust account and are generally not available to us for operating expenses, transaction costs, or other corporate purposes other than as specifically permitted by our governing documents. The funds available to us outside the trust account, together with any loans or advances from our sponsor and its affiliates, may be insufficient to fund our ongoing operations, conduct due diligence on prospective targets, negotiate and complete a business combination, and pay our general and administrative expenses. We have limited sources of revenue, and our existing cash resources outside the trust account may be depleted before we are able to consummate a business combination. If we are unable to obtain additional working capital from our sponsor or other sources, we may be required to curtail our search for a business combination target, reduce our operating activities, or liquidate earlier than anticipated. The limited availability of cash outside the trust account creates a risk that we may be unable to adequately evaluate prospective targets, fund necessary due diligence activities, or pay professional fees and expenses required to consummate a business combination. We are dependent on our sponsor for working capital support, and there can be no assurance that such support will be provided. Our ongoing operations have been funded primarily by loans and advances from our sponsor and its affiliates. Our sponsor is under no contractual or legal obligation to provide additional funding to us beyond what has already been committed. If our sponsor determines not to provide further working capital support, or is unable to do so due to its own financial constraints or other reasons, we may lack sufficient funds to continue our operations, pursue business combination opportunities, or satisfy our obligations as they become due. The reliance on our sponsor for working capital support also means that our ability to operate independently is limited. Decisions regarding the timing and amount of working capital contributions may be influenced by our sponsor’s own financial interests, the sponsor’s assessment of potential business combination opportunities, or the sponsor’s evaluation of the likelihood that we will successfully consummate a transaction. There can be no assurance that the interests of our sponsor in providing (or withholding) working capital support will align with the interests of our public shareholders. Insufficient funds outside the trust account may force us to liquidate earlier than planned, which could result in reduced distributions to public shareholders. If we exhaust our available cash resources outside the trust account and are unable to obtain additional financing from our sponsor or other sources, we may be unable to continue our search for a business combination target or fund the costs necessary to consummate a proposed transaction. In such circumstances, we may be forced to commence liquidation proceedings earlier than the deadline imposed by our governing documents. An early liquidation could result in reduced distributions to public shareholders because (i) we would have less time to allow interest to accrue on trust account funds, and (ii) the costs of an early liquidation, including professional fees and administrative expenses, would reduce the amount available for distribution. 42 Restrictions on the use of trust account funds limit our operational flexibility and our ability to pursue business combination opportunities. The funds in our trust account are subject to strict restrictions on use and may only be released in connection with the consummation of a business combination, shareholder redemptions, tax payments, and limited other permitted purposes as set forth in our governing documents and the trust agreement. These restrictions significantly limit our operational flexibility and our ability to deploy capital in pursuit of business combination opportunities. For example, we may not use trust account funds to pay deposits, fund due diligence expenses, or make preliminary investments in a target company prior to the closing of a business combination. Additionally, our inability to use trust account funds for general corporate purposes means that we are entirely reliant on funds outside the trust account and related-party financing for our day-to-day operations. If we are unable to secure sufficient funding from these limited sources, we may be unable to take advantage of business combination opportunities that arise, potentially resulting in our failure to consummate a transaction and our ultimate liquidation. Risks Relating to Potential Dilution from Rights and Future Financings The conversion of rights into shares of common stock upon consummation of a business combination will dilute the ownership interests of public shareholders. Each holder of a right included in the units sold in our initial public offering is entitled to receive a fraction of a share of common stock (for example, one-tenth of a share) upon the consummation of a business combination. The issuance of shares upon conversion of these rights will dilute the ownership interests of holders of our public shares and will increase the number of shares outstanding. The dilutive effect of the conversion of rights will reduce the per-share value of our common stock, and public shareholders who do not hold rights (or who hold fewer rights relative to their share ownership) will bear a disproportionate share of this dilution. Additionally, the conversion of rights upon a business combination is automatic and occurs without the payment of additional consideration by the rights holders. This means that the issuance of shares upon conversion of rights will increase the total number of shares outstanding without a corresponding increase in the aggregate value of the Company, resulting in dilution to all other shareholders. The issuance of founder shares to our sponsor at nominal cost creates significant dilution to public shareholders and may misalign incentives. Prior to our initial public offering, our sponsor was issued founder shares representing approximately 20% of our total outstanding shares of common stock following the offering, in exchange for nominal consideration. Following significant redemptions by public shareholders, only 6,969 public shares of common stock remain outstanding, which means the founder shares now represent a substantially larger percentage of our outstanding equity than they did at the time of the initial public offering. The disparity between the price paid by our sponsor for such shares and the price paid by our public shareholders in the initial public offering results in immediate and substantial dilution to public shareholders, and this dilutive effect has been significantly magnified by the reduction in public shares outstanding due to redemptions. The founder shares are BRAC common stock. At the Conwall Business Combination, each outstanding BRAC common share is to be exchanged for one Holdco Ordinary Share under the amended Business Combination Agreement; the Sponsor has waived its anti-dilution rights under the BRAC Charter. The existence of the founder shares may make it more difficult for us to consummate a Business Combination with a target company at a price that would deliver attractive returns to public shareholders, as the value represented by the founder shares must effectively be absorbed by the value of the combined company. Furthermore, because the founder shares were acquired at nominal cost, our sponsor may realize a positive return on its investment even if the per-share value of the post-combination company declines significantly below the per-share price paid by public shareholders. Future equity or convertible financings undertaken in connection with or following a business combination may result in additional dilution to public shareholders. In connection with a business combination, or following the consummation thereof, we may issue additional shares of common stock, preferred stock, convertible securities, or other equity-linked instruments to finance the transaction consideration, raise additional working capital, fund the operations of the post-combination company, or for other corporate purposes. Any such issuance will dilute the ownership interests of our existing shareholders, and the terms of such securities may include rights, preferences, or privileges that are senior to those of our common stock. There can be no assurance that future financing transactions will be completed on terms that are favorable to existing shareholders, and any dilutive financing could adversely affect the per-share value of our common stock. Additionally, we may issue equity or equity-linked securities to the sellers of a target business as part of the business combination consideration, to financial advisors or service providers as transaction fees, or to investors in a private investment in public equity (PIPE) transaction or similar financing. The aggregate dilutive effect of such issuances, together with the conversion of rights and the outstanding founder shares, could be substantial and could significantly reduce the percentage ownership of public shareholders in the post-combination company. Investors should be aware that they may experience significant dilution from multiple sources in connection with a business combination. Full protection cannot be assured: coverage remains subject to underwriting, exclusions, limits, retentions and the policy’s terms, and a new policy may not eliminate the existing coverage gap. The applicable closing condition may be waived only through the independent, disinterested board and audit-committee process specified in Section 9.2. Our project awards depend on competitive tendering and customer qualification requirements, and our historical quotation conversion rates are not indicative of future awards. If similar projects are not awarded, if customers delay capital expenditures, or if project completion percentages decline in future periods, our revenue and profitability could decrease materially. 45 We recognize revenue over time using the cost-to-cost method, and our results, contract balances and operating cash flows may vary significantly from period to period . Revenue is recognized over time using the cost-to-cost method, whereby project progress is measured by comparing costs incurred to date against the estimated total contract costs. As a result, our revenue, gross profit, contract assets, deferred revenue, retention receivables and operating cash flows depend on project commencement, progress toward completion, customer approvals, billing milestones, collection timing, procurement timing and subcontractor payment terms, and our results may vary significantly from period to period. Our contracts are typically billed through progress claims based on the value of work completed and certified by the client’s consultant. Progress payments are generally subject to a 5% retention, with 50% of the retention sum released upon issuance of the Certificate of Practical Completion (CPC) and the remaining 50% released upon expiry of the Defects Liability Period (DLP), subject to the applicable contractual provisions. Certified progress claims are generally payable within 30 to 60 days from the date of certification, although actual payment timing may vary depending on the client’s internal certification and payment approval processes. During periods of rapid project growth, our revenue and net income may increase while our operating cash flow declines if contract assets, accounts receivable, project retention or fixed deposits increase faster than customer collections. Changes in estimated total contract costs, disputed or unapproved variation orders, delayed certifications or slower collections could therefore materially affect our reported results, liquidity and working capital. Demand for our services depends substantially on industry capital expenditures, which are cyclical, difficult to predict and affected by customer investment decisions. The Company’s revenue and growth prospects are closely linked to capital expenditure programs of semiconductor manufacturers, integrated device manufacturers, foundries, outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) providers, memory manufacturers, advanced packaging companies and other technology customers. These customers periodically adjust facility-expansion, cleanroom, utility and infrastructure investments based on market demand, product pricing, inventory levels, profitability, financing conditions, technology roadmaps, geopolitical developments and macroeconomic conditions. A reduction, postponement or reprioritization of semiconductor capital expenditures could reduce bidding opportunities, delay contract awards, slow backlog conversion and adversely affect revenue, margins and cash flow. Semiconductor capital spending may decline during memory market downturns, periods of excess capacity, inventory corrections or budget reductions. The memory market, including dynamic random access memory (DRAM), NAND flash memory and high-bandwidth memory (HBM), has historically experienced significant pricing and demand volatility. If memory manufacturers or other semiconductor customers experience weaker demand, lower selling prices, excess inventory or lower utilization rates, they may defer facility expansions, cleanroom upgrades, process utility investments, equipment installation projects or manufacturing support infrastructure. Even where projects are ultimately completed, delays may disrupt resource planning, increase project costs and reduce the Company’s ability to utilize personnel and subcontractors efficiently. Increased AI adoption does not assure that customers will award contracts to the Company, that projects will be undertaken in the Company’s markets or that any awarded projects will be profitable. AI infrastructure investment is also subject to substantial timing and demand uncertainty. Hyperscale cloud providers, technology companies and data-center operators may reduce, delay or reprioritize capital expenditures based on profitability, utilization levels, return-on-investment expectations, financing conditions, power availability, regulatory constraints or changes in technology architecture. If AI adoption slows, customer spending becomes more disciplined or AI-related infrastructure buildout is reduced, semiconductor manufacturers and related customers may scale back expansion plans, which could reduce demand for the Company’s cleanroom, M&E, civil, structural and architectural (CSA), commissioning and facility-integration services. 46 Demand related to graphics processing units (GPUs), HBM and advanced packaging may fluctuate and may not translate into project awards or sustained growth. Overcapacity may arise when manufacturers, encouraged by AI-related demand, government incentives, supply-chain diversification initiatives or competitive pressures, add capacity faster than actual end-market demand develops. Excess capacity can reduce customer utilization, pricing power and profitability, causing customers to postpone expansion phases, defer new projects, reduce utility upgrades or prioritize operational efficiency over new facility investments. Substantially all of our revenue and operating costs are denominated in Malaysian ringgit, while we report our financial results in U.S. dollars. Appreciation or depreciation of the ringgit against the U.S. dollar affects our reported revenue, expenses, earnings, assets and liabilities, as well as the U.S. dollar value of any dividends or other distributions. The ringgit appreciated significantly against the U.S. dollar during 2025 and 2026, and market commentators have cautioned that a sharp correction in either direction is possible. In addition, Bank Negara Malaysia administers foreign exchange policy rules governing borrowing, investment abroad and the conversion and repatriation of proceeds, and has in recent periods encouraged the repatriation and conversion of foreign earnings by Malaysian corporations. Changes in those rules, including as a result of currency policy understandings under discussion between the U.S. Department of the Treasury and Bank Negara Malaysia, could restrict our ability to move funds within our group, hedge our exposures or pay dividends. A pending U.S. Section 232 investigation into semiconductor imports could result in additional duties that would directly affect back-end assembly, packaging and test operations in Malaysia, which are among the principal activities of the customers we serve. We depend on foreign labor, and increases in levies, quotas or immigration restrictions could increase our costs or delay our projects. Construction and installation work in Malaysia depends heavily on foreign workers. We utilize foreign labor through various arrangements, including foreign workers who perform work under our supervision and direction, as well as foreign workers engaged by our subcontractors or through third-party labor or outsourcing arrangements. The employment and deployment of foreign workers in Malaysia are subject to quotas, source-country arrangements, permit approvals and annual levies administered by the relevant Malaysian authorities. The annual levy for foreign workers in the construction sector in Peninsular Malaysia is currently RM1,850 per worker, in addition to visa and processing fees. The Malaysian government has also implemented a multi-tier levy framework under which the levy payable by employers may vary based on their reliance on foreign labor. Employer contribution obligations for foreign workers under the Employees Provident Fund and social security regimes have also been extended in recent years. Increases in levies, tightening of quotas, delays or suspensions in permit approvals and renewals, minimum wage revisions, changes in requirements applicable to foreign-worker arrangements, or the unavailability of workers from source countries could increase our direct or subcontracted labor costs, disrupt our access to foreign workers, delay project delivery, expose us to liquidated damages and reduce our margins. Cybersecurity incidents could disrupt our operations or expose confidential project information. We rely on information systems for engineering design, project management, procurement, financial reporting, customer communication and vendor coordination. Cyberattacks, ransomware, unauthorized access, data loss or system disruptions could delay projects, compromise confidential customer or supplier information, disrupt operations, increase costs and damage our reputation. Allegations of forced labor or non-compliant recruitment practices, whether by us or our subcontractors, could result in enforcement action, loss of customers and reputational harm. Multinational customers commonly impose responsible sourcing and labor standards audits on contractors and subcontractors working at their sites, and we may not be able to detect or prevent non-compliance by the labor suppliers and subcontractors we engage. Allegations or findings of forced labor or unlawful recruitment practices, whether or not substantiated and whether relating to us or to our subcontractors, could result in loss of customer qualification, contract termination, regulatory investigation, penalties, restrictions affecting our customers’ exports and significant reputational harm. BRAC Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations We are a blank check company formed under the laws of the State of Delaware on April 16, 2021, for the purpose of effecting a merger, capital stock exchange, asset acquisition, stock purchase, reorganization or other similar Business Combination with one or more businesses. We intend to effectuate our Business Combination using cash from the proceeds of the IPO and the sale of the private placement, our capital stock, debt or a combination of cash, stock and debt. The Company has not conducted any active operations since inception, except for its efforts to locate suitable acquisition candidates. No revenue has been generated by the Company since inception. It is unlikely the Company will have any revenues unless it is able to effect an acquisition or merger with an operating company, of which there can be no assurance. The Company’s plan of operation for the remainder of the fiscal year shall be to continue its efforts to locate suitable acquisition candidates. Our principal business objective for the next 12 months and beyond such time will be to achieve long-term growth potential through a combination with a business rather than immediate, short-term earnings. The Company will not restrict our potential candidate target companies to any specific business, industry or geographical location and, thus, may acquire any type of business. The costs of investigating and analyzing business combinations for the next 12 months and beyond such time will be paid with funds to be loaned to or invested in us by our stockholders, management or other investors. During the next 12 months we anticipate incurring costs related to: (i) filing of Exchange Act reports, and (ii) investigating, analyzing and consummating an acquisition. We cannot assure you that our plans to raise capital or to complete our initial Business Combination will be successful. Internal Control Over Financial Reporting In connection with the preparation and audit of the Company’s financial statements as of and for the year ended December 31, 2025, management identified material weaknesses in the Company’s internal control over financial reporting. The material weaknesses consisted of: (i) inadequate segregation of duties within accounting processes due to limited personnel; (ii) insufficient written policies and procedures for accounting, information technology, financial reporting and recordkeeping; (iii) a lack of controls over the financial reporting process that failed to recognize the accrual of penalties and interest on tax payables and resulted in the revision of previously issued financial statements; and (iv) a lack of controls to monitor compliance with the provisions of the Trust Agreement relating to the use of funds withdrawn from the Trust Account for payment of the Company’s tax liabilities. These material weaknesses increase the risk that a material misstatement of the Company’s annual or interim financial statements may not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis, and could result in additional revisions to the Company’s financial statements, additional penalties and interest on tax liabilities, or noncompliance with the Trust Agreement. The Company is an emerging growth company and is not required to have, and MaloneBailey, LLP was not engaged to perform, an audit of the effectiveness of the Company’s internal control over financial reporting. Accordingly, MaloneBailey, LLP did not express an opinion on the effectiveness of the Company’s internal control over financial reporting. Material Weaknesses in Internal Control Over Financial Reporting In connection with the preparation and audit of the Company’s financial statements as of and for the year ended December 31, 2025, management identified material weaknesses in the Company’s internal control over financial reporting. The material weaknesses related to inadequate segregation of duties within accounting processes due to limited personnel, insufficient written policies and procedures for accounting, information technology, financial reporting and recordkeeping, lack of controls over the financial reporting process that failed to recognize the accrual of penalties and interest on tax payables and resulted in revisions to previously issued financial statements, and lack of controls to monitor compliance with the provisions of the Trust Agreement related to the use of funds withdrawn from the Trust Account for payment of the Company’s tax liabilities. As a result of these material weaknesses, there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the Company’s annual or interim financial statements would not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis. The Company has begun evaluating remediation measures, including enhancing review controls over financial reporting, tax accruals and Trust Account withdrawals, and developing additional accounting, information technology, financial reporting and recordkeeping policies and procedures. The material weaknesses will not be considered remediated until the applicable controls have been designed, implemented and operated for a sufficient period of time and management has concluded, through testing, that the controls are operating effectively.
